# What Is Agent Washing?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agent washing is the practice of marketing existing assistants, chatbots or automation scripts as autonomous AI agents. Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic products offer genuine agentic features. Regulators already act against false AI claims, and buyers can test a vendor in one demo with five questions.

Agent washing is the practice of rebranding existing AI assistants, chatbots or robotic process automation (RPA) tools as "agentic AI" without adding real agent capabilities. Gartner, which uses the term in its agentic AI research, estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic products are genuine. For a buyer, the risk is paying agent prices for assistant behaviour. A short, structured demo usually exposes the difference.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What agent washing means

Gartner used the term in its June 2025 forecast on agentic AI. Its analysts observed that many vendors were contributing to market hype by rebranding existing products as agentic: AI assistants, chatbots and RPA tools. By its estimate, only about 130 of the thousands of vendors making agentic claims actually offer genuine agentic features.

The same forecast predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. Gartner's Anushree Verma said most agentic AI propositions "lack significant value or return on investment". Agent washing feeds that failure rate. A team that buys a relabelled chatbot expecting an agent will find the gap only after deployment.

The term borrows from "AI washing", a phrase regulators already use. In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers, Delphia and Global Predictions, for claiming AI capabilities they did not have. Then-chair Gary Gensler said: "Such AI washing hurts investors." In September 2024 the FTC announced Operation AI Comply, a set of actions against deceptive AI claims. Chair Lina Khan said there is "no AI exemption from the laws on the books."

| Genuine agent | Agent-washed product |
| --- | --- |
| Decides its own sequence of steps towards a goal | Follows a fixed script or decision tree |
| Chooses which tools to call based on the situation | Calls one integration in a predetermined order |
| Reads results and changes course when a step fails | Stops or returns an error when the script breaks |
| Can show a log of the steps it chose and why | Shows only the final output |
| Lets you set autonomy per task | Offers one mode: on |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial teams are a prime target. "AI SDR" and "autonomous agent" have become common labels on tools that schedule sequences or summarise calls. Those tools may be useful; the problem is the price and expectations the label brings.

Agent washing creates three specific costs. First, pricing: vendors often charge per agent or per outcome, which only makes sense if the product does the work of a person. Second, risk: a buyer who believes a tool will catch its own mistakes may give it more autonomy than it can handle. Third, opportunity: a team that spends a quarter discovering a product is a chatbot has lost a quarter on its first real agent.

There is a reverse problem too. Anthropic's guidance on building agents notes that many tasks are better served by a workflow, with steps fixed in code, than by a true agent. A relabelled workflow is not always a bad product. It is a mislabelled one, and should be priced and governed as what it is.

## How to test a vendor's agent claim

Five questions, asked in a live demo on your own data, separate most genuine agents from relabelled assistants.

| Question to ask | What a genuine agent shows | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Give it a goal it has not seen. What does it do?" | It plans steps and explains them | It asks for a template or a script |
| "Break one of its tools mid-task." | It notices and tries another route | It fails silently or stops |
| "Show me the log of what it chose and why." | A step-by-step trace with tool calls | A final answer only |
| "What can it never do, and where is that set?" | A configurable list of permissions | "It is safe by design" |
| "Which actions need a person to approve?" | Per-task autonomy settings | One global on/off switch |

Ask also how the vendor measures success: task completion and error rates on real work, not message counts.

Then write the answers down. In **lowob**'s view a buying decision is a record worth keeping: decision, reason, owner and expected outcome. If the product underperforms, the record shows whether the claim or the deployment was at fault.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat "agent" as a claim to test.** Gartner thinks most vendors using the label do not meet it.
- **Test on your data, live.** A goal the product has not seen, a broken tool and a request for the log reveal most washing.
- **Price what it is.** A relabelled workflow can be useful, but should not carry agent pricing or agent autonomy.
- **Record the decision.** Write down what the vendor claimed and what you expect, so the outcome can be checked.
